title: Progressive Disclosure — Skills as a Loading Strategy

questions.prompt: A 600-line skill has its three most important rules near the bottom. The session compacts. When the skill is re-attached, which content is most likely to be there?
options: The whole 600 lines, restored in full
Nothing — invoked skills are never re-attached
The first 5,000 tokens, filled from the top of the body
The bottom 5,000 tokens, because they were written most recently
questions.explanation: After compaction, Claude Code re-attaches the first 5,000 tokens of each invoked skill, with a 25,000-token combined budget. Option A overshoots — the cap exists because full restore is too expensive. Option B is wrong: invoked skills are re-attached; it is the *skill listing* that is not re-injected. Option D inverts the rule; the cap fills from the top of the file, which is why the strongest rule goes first.

questions.prompt: You want Claude to apply a set of codebase conventions automatically whenever they are relevant, but you do not want users to be able to trigger them with `/name`. Which frontmatter matches?
questions.explanation: `user-invocable: false` hides the skill from the `/` menu and stops `/name` from running it, while Claude can still invoke it — exactly the background-knowledge case. Option A is the reverse: it stops *Claude* from invoking on its own and leaves manual invocation open. Option C runs the skill in a forked subagent, which changes where it loads, not who can trigger it. Option D is a subagent-timing field that only applies with `context: fork`.

questions.prompt: You move a 400-line checklist out of a skill's body into `references/security.md` and add a one-line pointer. You invoke the skill for a tiny change that needs none of the checklist. What did the checklist cost this run?
options: 400 lines — files under the skill folder always ship into context
Nothing — supporting files are read only when the body points at them and they are actually read
Only the file's name, because the listing includes reference filenames
It is impossible to know without opening the file
questions.explanation: Supporting files are tier three: they cost nothing until the body points at them and something reads them. Option A is the misconception that a skill folder is a single blob. Option C invents a listing of reference filenames; the startup listing is skill name plus description only. Option D overstates the uncertainty — `/context` and the transcript show whether the file was read.

questions.prompt: You run `/compact` in a long session that had a dozen skills listed at startup. Which of these is true afterwards?
options: The skill descriptions reload with the rest of the startup content
The skill listing is not re-injected; only skills you actually invoked are carried forward
Every skill that was ever listed re-attaches in full
All skills are dropped, invoked or not
questions.explanation: The skill descriptions are the one startup block that does not re-inject after compaction; invoked skills are re-attached (first 5,000 tokens each). Option A assumes the listing behaves like `CLAUDE.md`, which does reload — it does not. Option C retells the whole-listing myth in reverse. Option D is too strong: invoked skills are preserved, which is the point of putting your strongest rule at the top.
